1:
That Paul calls himself a prisoner and not an apostle is noticed by everyone, and read two opposite ways. Ellicott sees a title appealing to sympathy substituted for one claiming authority, and observes that in the other letters of this captivity the chains are ground of glory, while here, in accordance with the writer's determination not to command but for love's sake to entreat, the other aspect has almost exclusive prominence. Robertson agrees the word is chosen on purpose as more effective with Philemon, and adds that Paul writes with a manacled right hand. Calvin takes it the other way: the chains were the badges of his embassy for Christ, and he names them to strengthen his authority, not from fear of being despised, since Philemon revered him, but because he was about to plead a runaway's cause. Chrysostom describes the effect rather than the intent: at the outset Paul has pulled down the master's spirit and quenched his anger, striking him with compunction by calling himself a prisoner.

Calvin opens with an estimate of the letter. The singular loftiness of Paul's mind, better seen elsewhere in weightier matters, is attested here too, for while handling a subject otherwise low and mean he rises to God with his wonted elevation; pleading for a runaway he seems to speak of the whole Church's interests rather than one man's affairs, and in behalf of a person of the lowest condition demeans himself so modestly that nowhere else is the meekness of his temper painted more vividly. Clarke turns the same oddity into a question about the canon: it may be thought strange that a short letter on a private subject, defending no doctrine, should from the highest antiquity have been received as Scripture; and he adds a striking piece of evidence, that it was held so sacred that even the ancient heretics never attempted to impugn or corrupt it, while making dangerously free with the Gospels and all the other epistles.

What Philemon was divides two of them. Clarke reports the guesses that he was bishop, elder or deacon, says there is no evidence for any, and concludes he was probably a private member whose house, hand and property were consecrated to God, his Church and the poor; on which he reflects that such a man need not envy the highest ecclesiastic. Calvin holds the opposite, that Philemon probably belonged to the order of pastors, since fellow-labourer is a title Paul does not bestow on a private individual. On Archippus they converge, Ellicott noting that fellow-soldier is used elsewhere only of Epaphroditus and seems to denote ministerial office, and Calvin that though every Christian is a soldier, teachers are standard-bearers whom Satan troubles more.

The other names are handled as evidence. Ellicott says Apphia is usually taken for the Roman Appia, but that such a name in a Greek-Asiatic family is improbable, and that the form Apphia occurs in many Phrygian inscriptions and may be native; Robertson confirms the inscriptions, and both take her for Philemon's wife. Ellicott conjectures Archippus was the son, while Robertson leaves it uncertain and suggests he may have been pastor at Colossae. The house church draws the best note: Robertson observes that before the third century there is no certain evidence of special buildings for worship, and lists the parallels at Jerusalem, Ephesus, Rome and Laodicea. Ellicott warns that the domestic character of the letter need not limit the phrase to Philemon's own family. Calvin makes it praise, that it is no small thing in a householder so to regulate his family as to be an image of the Church; Henry says the same of the honour done a house where God is worshipped and the members of Christ are welcome. Gill and Barnes fill in the salutation, Barnes noting that grace and peace joins the Greek greeting to the Hebrew.
4:
Chrysostom reads the thanksgiving as strategy, and describes the letter's whole shape from it. Paul does not ask the favour at the outset, but first admires the man, praises his good actions, proves his love by always mentioning him in prayer, says that many are refreshed by him, and only then puts the request last of all, by that placing putting him to the blush; for if others obtain what they ask, much more Paul, and if he were worthy coming first, much more coming after others and asking nothing for himself. He adds that Paul assigns other causes for the letter, lest anyone say that but for the slave he would not have written. Calvin draws a different lesson from the same verse, that Paul prays for the very thing he gives thanks for, since the most perfect, while they live here, never have such ground of congratulation as to need no prayers.

The next clause is a knot, because faith is said to be toward the saints. Ellicott sets out three ways of untying it: that faith here means fidelity, rejected as impossible for so nearly technical a phrase; that the two prepositions differ, one signifying direction and the other contact, so that faith has Christ for object but shows itself towards the saints, which he calls too artificial for such a letter; and, as he prefers, that the Colossian parallel settles it, the words standing in chiasmus. Robertson calls it momentum, Paul carrying both nouns over to the saints, while allowing chiasm too. Clarke reports that several excellent manuscripts put faith before love, which reads more naturally, and remarks that no figure of speech would vindicate saying faith in the saints. Calvin concedes the arrangement is confused but denies any obscurity of meaning.

What the communication of his faith means divides them three ways. Clarke takes it of almsgiving, citing Theophylact that almsgiving is so called because it is the fruit of much faith, and reports two variants, one reading evident for effectual, which he thinks agrees best with the scope of the place, and the better manuscripts reading in us for in you. Calvin denies the verse is praise at all, referring it to the prayer, and takes the sense to be that faith, communicating itself by good works, may be proved effectual, since though it has a hidden residence in the heart it makes itself known by actual effects; he adds that he would rather render the last phrase in Christ, but did not venture to alter the words and only mentions it so that readers may choose. Ellicott keeps the usual sense of fellowship, and asks with whom, answering, with both God and man; for the soul that dwells alone with God even in the holiest seclusion knows what is good in the abstract but not what is good in man in the concrete reality, whereas Philemon's house was a centre of Christian life.

The refreshing of the saints closes the thanksgiving. Ellicott notes that the verb is the very word of the promise to those who travail and are heavy laden, so that hearts are ultimately refreshed in Christ, though here through Philemon; Paul uses it elsewhere of the relief given by Christian fellowship on earth, while the Apocalypse applies it to rest with Christ in heaven. On the address brother Ellicott finds a marked emphasis of affection, the intimacy formed perhaps at Ephesus rather than Colossae, and suggests Philemon was Paul's equal in age, since although his convert he is never called his son in the faith. Robertson supplies the channel, that Paul heard through Epaphras and perhaps Onesimus, and gives the word rendered effectual its ordinary life, the papyri using it of a mill in working order. Gill and Barnes keep it pastoral, Barnes observing that Paul thanks God for what is good in men rather than praising them for it.
8:
That Paul has the right and declines to use it is the hinge, and each treats it as a lesson in authority. Robertson puts the grammar shortly, a concessive participle followed by a verb of entreaty rather than of command, which he had a perfect right to use. Calvin makes it a rule for pastors: he claims nothing except in Christ, on account of the office received from him, which shows that teachers may enact not whatever they please but only what is proper; and since men ready of their own accord listen more willingly to a calm statement of what must be done than to authority, pastors should draw disciples gently rather than drag them, for in foregoing his right by entreaty a man has far greater power to obtain his wish than by commanding. Calvin adds the balancing caution, that those treated so gently have nothing less exacted of them than what they owe. Henry counts the appeal out argument by argument, from the good already reported of Philemon, from the authority the apostle holds, from the waiving of it, from the circumstances of the man pleading, and from the new relation between writer and slave; and he draws the same moral, that it is no disparagement for the powerful to beseech where in strictness of right they might command.

Clarke gives the paragraph over to a long appreciation of the letter's art. The tenderness of the epistle has long been admired, yet the character of the apostle prevails throughout: the warm, affectionate, authoritative teacher is interceding with an absent friend for a beloved convert, with an earnestness befitting not so much the occasion as the ardour of his own mind. He shows himself conscious of the weight of his mission and does not let Philemon forget it, recalling obliquely the obligation under which he had laid him by bringing him to Christ. Without laying aside the apostolic character he softens the imperative style by mixing with it every consideration that could move his correspondent; aged and in prison, he is content to supplicate, and everything was to be voluntary. The observation is extended to the other letters, that such appeals to feeling, drawn mostly from his own sufferings, usually precede a command, soften a rebuke, or mitigate some disagreeable truth.

Paul the aged then produces the chapter's best philological knot, and it is worked four ways. Clarke computes that if the apostle were about twenty-five at the stoning of Stephen he could be no more than fifty-six here, which alone would not make him aged in our sense; but the word also means ambassador, since elderly men were chosen for that office, and the Septuagint uses the one form for the other, so that some would render it Paul the ambassador, which he thinks agrees well with the design of the place. Robertson supplies the technical support and then declines it: the papyri use the word of an old man, Hippocrates reckoning a man so from forty-nine to fifty-six, while the parallel about being an ambassador in a chain leads Lightfoot to hold that scribes confused the two words here, the Septuagint using them interchangeably four times; ambassador is undoubtedly possible, he grants, though there is no real reason why Paul should not properly call himself aged. Barnes assembles the chronology most fully, reporting one estimate of twenty-four at the stoning, making him fifty-three now, and another of thirty-five at his conversion, making him sixty-three, with the ancient definitions from Phavorinus and Varro; his own judgement is near sixty, with the qualification that a constitution much broken by labours and perils may give a man well short of the usual limit of life all the characteristics of great age. Calvin cuts across all three, holding that the designation denotes not age at all but office. Gill keeps to the plain reading of an old man pleading.
10:
The order of the words is itself noticed. Ellicott points out that the name is withheld until Philemon's interest is doubly engaged, first for one who is the apostle's own child, a term of endearment given elsewhere only to Timothy and Titus, and then for one begotten under the hardships of imprisonment; only at last does the name come, and even then in the same breath with the declaration of a change from past uselessness to present usefulness. Calvin dwells on the same title from the other side, marking how deep the condescension is that gives the name of son to a slave, a runaway and a thief; and he guards the metaphor, that the begetting was by Paul's ministry and not by his power, since to renew a soul to the image of God is no human work, yet because faith comes by hearing and the word preached is the seed of eternal life, he from whose mouth we receive that seed is rightly called a father, which implies no opposition between God and man but shows what God does by means of men. Robertson says simply that Paul is evidently proud of having won Onesimus while a prisoner himself.

The play on the name is agreed and its history disputed. Ellicott says the name means useful or profitable, though formed from a different root than the words used here, and that it is hardly possible not to see a play on words in the passage, adding, curiously enough, that the old Greek commentators do not notice it; his paraphrase is that Onesimus belied his name in days past and will more than deserve it now. Robertson finds the play doubled, in the adjective for useless and the compound for useful, and observes that the name was common among slaves. Clarke marks the allusion in one line, noting that the apostle uses a different Greek word to express the idea. Ellicott adds that of Onesimus himself we know absolutely nothing beyond this letter and the notice in Colossians, and that tradition has made him bishop of Beroea or identified him with the bishop of Ephesus named in an Ignatian letter.

Sending him back raises the question that governs the rest of the letter, and Clarke states the principle flatly: the Christian religion never cancels any civil relations, so that a slave on being converted has no right on that ground to claim emancipation from his master's service; justice therefore required that Onesimus be sent back, while love to the servant induced the apostle to write this conciliating letter. Calvin makes the appeal turn on affection rather than principle, that nothing could have been more powerful for assuaging Philemon's wrath, since to refuse forgiveness would have been cruelty against Paul's own bowels; and he draws the application, that if the conversion of a man to God were estimated by us at its proper value we too would so embrace those who give evidence of sincere repentance. Ellicott notes that the word receive is absent from the best manuscripts, supplied from a later verse to fill a broken construction, and then finds two distinctions in what follows, the first verb meaning to wish and the second to will, and the first standing in the imperfect against the past definite, I determined finally. On the phrase in thy stead he observes that a slave was his master's property and could act only on his master's behalf and by his consent, and on the next verse that Paul will not keep the man and ask that consent by letter, lest the benefit should wear even the semblance of constraint. Robertson notes the epistolary aorist, the sending described as it will look when Onesimus arrives, and says the apostle almost loves him as his own son. Gill and Barnes keep to the sense, Barnes observing that the whole leaves Philemon entirely free.
15:
The word perhaps is read by everyone as reverence rather than doubt. Gill says the apostle is softening the business, calling it not a running away but a departure for a little while, and suggesting an overruling providence such as attended Joseph's going down into Egypt. Barnes puts it as a possibility permitted in providence, that what appeared a calamity and a wrong might have been allowed so that Philemon should receive a higher benefit. Ellicott notes that the verb is passive, was parted rather than departed, a phrase not only euphemistic but suggesting that the flight was, however unconsciously, overruled by a higher hand. Clarke calls it another most delicate stroke: he departed an unfaithful slave and returns a beloved brother, so that Philemon has reason to be thankful he did depart; and Clarke, like Calvin, sets the whole beside Joseph's apology for his brethren. Calvin draws the general rule, that anger at offences ought to be soothed on perceiving that what was done through malice has been turned to another end by the purpose of God.

On the contrast of a season with for ever the readings part slightly. Ellicott observes that the word is the one always used for eternal, and that though the contrast might be satisfied by the merely relative sense of lifelong service, the phrase stands in direct reference to the brotherhood of the Communion of Saints and is better taken absolutely, of fellowship in the life eternal. Robertson agrees, eternal here and hereafter, and calls it a word that would touch the best in Philemon. Calvin keeps the contrast on the plainer level, that Onesimus while a runaway at heart was not actually enjoyed by his master even when in the house, and that the perpetuity of the gain is set against the short duration of the loss. Barnes takes the eternal sense and presses it into affection, binding the two in the bonds of love in a world that shall never end.

The next clause is where the commentators divide most sharply, and the dispute is over the word rendered servant. Barnes argues at length that it means servant of any kind, that it should never be assumed those to whom it is applied were slaves, and that all the evidence Onesimus was one lies in this single word, while the mention of owing suggests a man able to hold property. Robertson answers flatly that here it has to be slave, and says so it should be always. Clarke agrees the man was a part of Philemon's property, and Calvin speaks of a worthless slave and of dispositions so wicked that scarcely one in a hundred proved of real use, which makes the repentance the more memorable. Ellicott stands apart from both sides by locating in the verse the principle he calls absolutely destructive of the condition of slavery, and sets it out in three steps: the living chattel of inhuman laws is first a brother, united to his master by ties of ultimate equality and so having rights as well as duties; he is next a brother beloved, the natural tie made living by a love willing to sacrifice even its own rights; and above all this is in the Lord, the man bought by Christ's blood and made a son of God, so that to outrage him is an outrage towards Christ. Robertson quotes the same balance in a sentence he takes from Meyer, that in the flesh Philemon had the brother for a slave and in the Lord he had the slave for a brother. Henry, in the concise exposition attached here, states the principle they all in fact share, that Christianity does not do away our duties to others but directs to the right doing of them, and that the communion of saints does not destroy distinction of property.
17:
The word partner carries the weight of the appeal, and its rarity is noticed. Ellicott says the title is peculiar, nowhere else found in the singular and in absolute use except where Titus is called Paul's partner and fellow helper, and there the context ties it to the collection of alms; here it can hardly mean general Christian fellowship, which would need some such addition as in Christ, and must indicate a particular bond, since Philemon, though Paul's convert, is addressed not as a son but as a brother. Gill takes it more broadly, a companion who reckons the other's affairs and interest his own, a partner in grace and in the ministry, and notes that the word answers to one often used in the Talmudic writings for an associate of the doctors. Barnes rests it on the root, having something in common, common principles, common attachments, a common hope, so that if Philemon counted Paul such a man he must receive Onesimus on the same ground. Chrysostom admires the arrangement rather than the word: no procedure is so apt to gain a hearing as not to ask for everything at once, and only after my son, and partaker of the Gospel, and my bowels, and as a brother, does he add as myself. Robertson calls the same words a death-knell of human slavery wherever the spirit of Christ has its way. Calvin sees Paul lowering himself further, giving up his right and his honour to a runaway and putting him in his own room, because he reckoned it of vast importance that Onesimus should have a mild master lest immoderate severity drive him to despair.

Two commentators reach independently for the same classical parallel. Barnes points to the ninth letter of the first book of Horace as a plea in behalf of another strongly resembling this one; Clarke prints it in full, the recommendation of Septimius to Claudius Nero, calls it written with much art but greatly exceeded by Paul, and adds that Paul is also outdone by a letter of Pliny to Sabinianus on behalf of a servant who had incurred his master's displeasure. Chrysostom is watching the placing of the injury: see where and when he introduces the mention of it, last, after so many things said in the man's behalf, and note that he does not say if he has stolen anything but if he has wronged thee, at once confessing the offence and treating it as the wrong of a friend against a friend rather than of a servant.

The note of hand divides them. Ellicott says Paul introduces a regular bond couched in legal form, and infers that the apostle had money he could rightly call his own, most likely the offerings from Philippi, which were given freely and might fairly be spent on his own son in the faith. Robertson calls it Paul's promissory note, written with his own hand and collectable, and observes how many of the papyri concern debts. Calvin raises the difficulty squarely: how does a man who without the help of the churches had not the means of living frugally promise to pay money? Amidst such poverty the promise would be ridiculous, so that without irony, by an indirect figure, Paul is asking Philemon to blot out and cancel the account, since he who claims the whole man as his property need not trouble himself about paying. Gill allows that the thing written may have been a separate bill sent along with Onesimus. Barnes uses the verb, which occurs elsewhere only once, to argue that reckoning to an account never charges a man with what is not his own act or what he has not assumed, and that since Paul's consent was necessary here the case proves only that a man who voluntarily takes a wrong upon himself may be held answerable for it.
20:
The name is played on a third time and nobody misses it. Clarke says the phrase should be rendered let me have profit of thee and calls it an evident play on the name of Onesimus. Ellicott says the same, adds that the word is used of the mingled pleasure and help derived from children, and that the pronoun is emphatic, and paraphrases: may I find thee, as I have found him, a true Onesimus. Robertson notes the optative, the regular construction for a wish about the future, and Barnes explains the request to refresh the bowels, the seat of the affections, as asking that his own anxious feelings be set at rest. The next verse is where the two long views of the letter part. Calvin infers from the whole that the faith of the gospel does not overturn civil government or set aside the authority of masters over slaves, since Philemon, no ordinary man but a fellow labourer of Paul, is not stripped of the power the law allowed him but only asked to forgive and restore. Robertson reads the confidence in obedience the other way, that Paul knows Philemon will set Onesimus free and prefers that it come as Philemon's own wish rather than as a command, and he answers the criticism that Paul did not denounce slavery in plain terms by asking who, considering the actual conditions of the empire, could suggest a better plan for its ultimate overthrow. Clarke reports that some think the apostle hints at manumission.

The request for a lodging is read as part of the persuasion. Gill says nothing grand was expected, a room such as the Shunamite furnished for the man of God would have contented him, and the hint was dropped to stir Philemon to receive the servant the sooner, since a man who thought he would never see the apostle again might be negligent. Barnes and Clarke both take the expectation of release as genuine and near, Clarke dating the letter shortly before the end of the first Roman imprisonment, asking whether the request is not itself a way of conferring an obligation, and adding that some think Paul wished a house hired for him at Colosse. Calvin admits we do not know whether Paul was ever released, and finds no absurdity even if he was disappointed of a hope about God's temporal kindness, since he had no confident hope of release further than if it pleased God and kept his mind in suspense until the result declared the will of God; and Calvin draws from the phrase through your prayers the note that what believers obtain by praying is said to be given them, from which we infer that our prayers, though not unsuccessful, have no power through their own merit.

The greetings raise one small question and the close a large one. Whether Epaphras was literally a fellow prisoner is disputed: Barnes thinks nothing more probable though Colossians does not mention it, Clarke says the silence does not settle the matter, and Robertson takes the word metaphorically while noting that some hold he was imprisoned with Paul at Rome. Calvin, reaching Demas, remembers the later desertion and warns that if an assistant of Paul was drawn aside by the vanity of the world, no man should reckon too confidently on the zeal of a single year. Both Barnes and Clarke close by printing Pliny's letter to Sabinianus pleading for a freedman, and Clarke adds the second letter thanking him for relenting, judging that Paul has the advantage only because he had Christian motives to urge. Barnes ends on the argument that a system which the spread of the gospel would destroy cannot be right now, since Christianity annihilates nothing that is good. Henry closes where the letter does, that grace is the best wish for ourselves and others, and with this the apostle begins and ends.
